articles.title: Hallowarrior review – apocalyptic Home Alone-style survival horror delivers inventive shocks
articles.summary: Debut feature from Ben Sottak provides outlandish Halloween-based scares, with Milly Shapiro superb as the naive yet resilient home-defender, Pumpkin. Home Alone meets Mad Max in this atmospheric seasonal chiller, named for Halloween and not a cheery greeting.
body: It’s the first major screen role for Shapiro since her memorable debut as the little sister in Ari Aster’s Hereditary, and she is in almost every scene here, making for quite the showcase. It’s good casting: Pumpkin is an intriguing presence – at once young and old, presumably because she’s been fending for herself during such a key stage of her development. She’s not had any adult guidance since the age of 12 – arresting her development in some ways, while having to survive, be totally independent and grieve her entire family alone has simultaneously made her unusually tough in others.
points: Debut feature from Ben Sottak provides outlandish Halloween-based scares, with Milly Shapiro superb as the naive yet resilient home-defender, Pumpkin.
Home Alone meets Mad Max in this atmospheric seasonal chiller, named for Halloween and not a cheery greeting.

articles.title: ‘A rare indulgence’: why Black Swan is my feelgood movie
articles.summary: The latest in our series of writers explaining their go-to comfort films is a tribute to Darren Aronofsky’s dark and unusually satisfying ballet nightmare. In early 2011, sometime after the film was released on home video, I sat down with mum to watch what she had heard was a “new ballet movie” by…
body: Well before Brendan Fraser’s time on the couch and the many houseguests of Mother!, Aronofsky increased the wattage with a companion piece to follow his heavy-hitter, The Wrestler. Watching Nina Sayers’ (Portman) intense physical trials and her stilted sexual awakening, with my mum beside me, I was understandably disturbed. At this point in my adolescence, I thought Jumanji was a scary movie. Like the film’s injured bird, I was being introduced to a darkness I didn’t understand. And somehow I couldn’t get enough. Why did it feel so good?

In the years since, I have returned to Black Swan in search of that same dread and delight. With each viewing, my affection for it deepens. The pale pinks and gentle powdery blues, Nina’s cosy wrap sweaters and leotards, even Barbara Hershey’s smothering presence, all of it has become an unexpected comfort.

articles.title: Deadline review – shocking threat sends tremors through authoritarian school
articles.summary: Set in a dystopian private academy rife with surveillance and cut-throat competition, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama cements his status as an important film-maker. Filmed in Taiwan and set entirely inside a prestigious high school, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama frames educational systems not merely as a…
body: This panopticon atmosphere of surveillance and cut-throat competition is punctured by a shocking incident: an anonymous student drops a flurry of leaflets announcing their intent to take their own life on the day of the final exam, unless the school changes its authoritarian ways. The note sends tremors through both the administration and the students; intersecting narrative lines weave through a group of characters that include a model student, a dedicated but ambivalent teacher and a righteous slacker. Each carries a heavy secret that points to the moral rot beneath the facade of academic excellence.

articles.title: Tense Presidential Elections, a Focus on Domestic Audiences and Oscars Closer Than Ever: 10 Takeaways From the Rio Film Festival
articles.summary: Hosting a film festival during historic presidential elections destined to shape an entire country’s future is a hefty ask, but this year’s Rio Film Festival managed to carefully and purposefully thread the lines between focusing on the cinema and the industry of today and not turning a blind eye…
body: Despite the tensions brought up by the elections, there was a latent sense of camaraderie and hope at the festival in the days since the first round at the polls. Several filmmakers have taken up to the stage at the festival to declare their support of Lula, including “Club Kid” director Jordan Firstman, who raised his hand into an “L” sign while introducing the festival’s closing film at the Odeon on Saturday night.

At several of this year’s panels at the festival’s industry sidebar, RioMarket, key executives and producers frequently mentioned the need for audience development in Brazil. The consensus was that the country offers already eager cinephiles, with many young audiences well-versed in international cinema thanks to healthy online communities, but there is still a challenge when it comes to converting those film fans into cinema-goers. In one of the festival’s first industry sessions, an in-conversation event with director Marcelo Gomes and Rodrigo Santoro, festival director Ilda Santiago brought up a burning issue: the still small number of cinema theater screens in Brazil.

articles.title: Piracy in the Crosshairs: Brazil to Launch Campaign Against IP Theft
articles.summary: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Brazil’s Audiovisual Industry and Commerce Federation (FICA) announced at the Rio Film Festival’s RioMarket the launch at the end of October of an anti-piracy awareness campaign in free-to-air and pay television, radio, out-of-home (OOH) advertising and movie theaters.
body: Disque Denúncia, a Brazilian anonymous crime-reporting hotline, is a campaign partner. The initiative allows citizens to report suspected criminal activities without revealing their identities.
Bastos said the campaign will use the language of films and series to communicate the danger of piracy. They created pirate characters for the campaign inspired by pirate productions.

“Anti-piracy campaigns generally adopt a law-enforcement tone, emphasizing repression, which tends to alienate audiences. We chose a cinematic approach instead, drawing inspiration from pirate productions,” Bastos said.

A 2022 study of Brazil’s Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) pointed out that piracy caused annual losses of 12 billion reais ($2.4 billion) in the country, Jonas Antunes Couto, president of the Brazilian Pay-TV Association ( ABTA ), told Variety. The study also identified piracy practices in about 4.5 million households in Brazil.

articles.title: Pasto Cine Boards ‘Puan’ Helmer María Alché’s ‘I Love You and Today Everything Looks Beautiful’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Argentina’s Pasto Cine has boarded María Alché’s upcoming “I Love You and Today Everything Looks Beautiful.” The film is produced by leading Brazilian banner Bubbles Project alongside Spain’s Elastica Films, Germany’s Pandora Film, and France’s Maneki Films.
body: Actress, screenwriter, and director Alché wrote and directed “Puan” alongside Benjamín Naishtat (“Glaxo”). The film won the Silver Shell for Actor and Screenplay at the San Sebastián Film Festival, was nominated for the Goya Awards, and was a box office hit in Argentina.

She co-wrote Lucrecia Martel’s “Nuestra tierra” and wrote and directed the feature film “A Family Submerged,” which won the Horizontes Latinos Award in San Sebastián, the Ingmar Bergman Award for Best First Feature at the Goteborg Film Festival, Best Screenplay at the Lima Film Festival, and Best Director at Ficunam.

Alché’s latest is currently in the financing stages and is aiming to shoot in the second half of 2027. Renowned French cinematographer Hélène Louvart (“La Chimera,” “The Lost Daughter”) has also joined the project, as have “Divine Love” editor Livia Serpa and “I’m Still Here” sound director Laura Zimerman. This is the third collaboration between the Argentinian director and Tatiana Leite’s Bubbles Project, and the fourth collaboration between Bubbles and Barbara Francisco’s Pasto Cine.

articles.title: ‘Silver Express’ Review: Miki Tanaka’s Sensitive Debut Feature Explores Asexual and Aromantic Identity
articles.summary: There are films and series with asexual characters in them, but far fewer interested in the experiential questions about moving through society as asexual and aromantic, and considering that identity on a spectrum.
body: Yui Okamoto and Hayato Kurihara's performances bolster an understated story that chafes at societal conditioning around hetero-coupledom.

While it does consider a sort of struggling common language (or at least, a definitive shorthand) around asexuality, “Silver Express” is for the most part interested in how that hazy definition, or continuing adjustment to a definition, is experienced on a personal level, as the loneliness of moving against the current. Tanaka’s film doesn’t assume that platonic relationships between men and women are a pipe dream — it just so happens that Chieri keeps running into people with “ulterior motives.”

The film moves at a casual clip, as conversations and relationships flow quickly across days and locations. The elliptical passage of time across the film’s broader structure also manifests more directly in how Tanaka shapes a scene, sometimes cutting off before the final word spoken.

articles.title: A Fidai Film review – Palestinian collage film transforms suppressed footage into works of art
articles.summary: Using archive material of destroyed houses, terrorised children and dead bodies, Kamal Aljafari adds humanity to the reels by overlaying poems by Palestinian authors. In Arabic, “fidai” means someone willing to sacrifice themselves for the greater good.
body: More than simply a work of compilation, the film also performs its own historical intervention. Many of the reels are imprinted with pejorative captions added by Israeli authorities, which Aljafari covers in streaks of red paint. In their place are excerpts from poems by Palestinian authors such as Ghassan Kanafani, whose words return a sense of humanity to these past images. Through these strategies of reclamation, Aljafari’s film brings liberation, if only momentarily, to a captive archive.

articles.title: Russell Brand arrives at court for start of rape trial
articles.summary: The 51-year-old actor and comedian denies charges of rape and sexual assault against six women.
body: Russell Brand has arrived at court for the start of his rape and sexual assault trial.

The 51-year-old comedian and actor has been charged with three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault, which are alleged to have occurred between 1999 and 2009.
The trial at Southwark Crown Court, which could last up to 10 weeks, is expected to begin with the process of jury selection on Monday morning.
The comedian and actor arrived at court wearing a navy suit and sunglasses, accompanied by his wife Laura.

articles.title: ‘Rebellion’: Why the Bradford 12 Doc Is So Timely and Its Directors Want People to Know “Your Problems Are Created by Elon Musk, Not Migrants”
articles.summary: Ken Fero discusses the London-premiering story of young South Asian men who stood trial on terrorism charges for preparing to defend their community from a racist attack, co-directed with one of them.
body: Bradford, near Leeds, is a city in the north of England. During the Industrial Revolution, it was known as THE place for wool manufacturing. Nowadays, it has a reputation for its South Asian food scene, among other things.

Rebellion world-premieres as part of the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF) on Oct. 14. “Revolution is the beat that drums through this electrifying story about the landmark case against the Bradford 12,” the festival website notes.

Fero talked to THR about how timely Rebellion feels today amid a renewed rise of far-right politics, why it was a journey of more than 30 years, the importance of involving the community in making the film and why cinema can be a weapon.
Rebellion feels very timely. How long did you work on it, and did you know early on that this would be a historic film that also reflects on our presence?
